title: Body cues, not facial expressions, discriminate between intense positive and negative emotions.

sources.title: Camerer et al. Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015
sources.finding: The preregistered independent replication reports positive significant focal results for both Aviezer and Karpicke/Blunt in Figure 1. Original-author reviewed protocols; not every original experiment was repeated.

sources.title: Pillaud, Chassaing-Monjou and Cottin: I React to Bodies but not Faces, Replication and Extension of Aviezer et al., 2012
sources.finding: Conference author abstract page 178 reports a preregistered independent replication of Experiment 1 (N=194) plus four affective-task extensions. Bodies rather than isolated faces discriminate peak-emotion valence. Conference report; not full methods.

sources.title: Pillaud et al. I react to bodies but not faces, a replication and extension of Aviezer et al. (2012), Emotion, doi:10.1037/emo0001621
sources.finding: Read the complete author abstract as indexed by OpenAlex: five experiments replicate Experiment 1 and extend to affective priming, misattribution, feelings and action tendencies; body-only stimuli consistently produce the effects. Same research program as P, not a third group.

No read independent synthesis or operational implementation established; original broader mimicry claims not all directly retested.
summary: The focal peak-emotion body-cue result replicated independently and supported new affective-task experiments. Operational use, explicit tests of every limitation, and adoption in a read synthesis remain unestablished.
researcher: Codex independent blind repeat by expand_manylabs; first grade not viewed
central_claims: At peak emotion intensity bodies discriminate positive/negative events better than faces.
Body context shifts perceived facial emotion and mimicry.
